common_name: Fastigiata Ginkgo (Narrow Columnar Male Maidenhair Tree)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring or fall in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun; Fastigiata is one of the oldest named ginkgo selections, an all-male clone grown for over a century for its narrow, densely upright columnar habit.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun, watering regularly through the first two to three seasons to help the young tree establish; mature ginkgo are exceptionally tough and tolerate heat, drought, pollution, and compacted urban soils with ease. Fastigiata is among the earliest-named ginkgo cultivars in Western cultivation, valued for over a hundred years for its narrowly conical to columnar habit, only slightly broader at the base, that fits tight side yards, allees, and street strips where a wide-spreading shade tree would not. Like other columnar forms it is propagated as an all-male clone, so it never produces the malodorous, messy fruit borne by female ginkgo trees. Foliage is the classic fan-shaped ginkgo leaf, turning a vivid clear gold in autumn before dropping over a short window. Ginkgo is essentially free of serious insect and disease problems, and little pruning is needed beyond removing any dead or crossing branches while the tree is young.

common_name: Chi Chi Ginkgo (Dwarf Mounded Shrub-Form Male Maidenhair Tree)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun; Chi Chi is a slow-growing, multi-stemmed dwarf male clone that stays a dense mounded shrub rather than developing into a tree.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun; Chi Chi tolerates a wide range of soils including alkaline and compacted urban ground, and is notably resistant to drought, pollution, salt, and deer browsing once established. This dwarf, dense, multi-stemmed male clone grows very slowly into a mounded, fan-shaped shrub, typically reaching only about 4 to 5 feet tall after a decade, making it useful in foundation plantings, rock gardens, and small landscapes where a full-size ginkgo tree would not fit. The cultivar name references the unusual swellings, clusters of dormant buds called 'chichi,' that develop on the bark of older branches. Foliage is the typical bright green ginkgo fan leaf, turning uniform gold each fall. Being a male selection, Chi Chi never sets the odorous fruit borne by female trees. It is essentially pest- and disease-free and needs only minimal pruning to remove dead or crossing wood.

common_name: Mariken Ginkgo (Dwarf Weeping Groundcover Male Maidenhair Tree)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Mariken is an extremely slow-growing witch's-broom sport of ginkgo discovered in Holland in 1995, staying a low, weeping mound for many years.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Mariken is easy to grow, deer-resistant, and tolerant of urban pollution once established, though it appreciates more consistent moisture than a full-size ginkgo. Discovered as a witch's-broom mutation in the Netherlands in 1995, this dwarf male cultivar grows extremely slowly into a low, somewhat weeping mound, reaching only about 2 feet tall by 2 feet wide after ten years and eventually spreading wider than tall with age. Small, ruffled, cupped leaves emerge celery-green and turn golden yellow in autumn, echoing the fall color of the species in miniature. Its low, spreading habit and slow growth make it a favorite for containers, rock gardens, bonsai training, and small-space patio plantings. As a male clone it produces no fruit, and like all ginkgo it is essentially untroubled by pests or disease.

common_name: Golden Girl Ginkgo (Female Nut-Producing Maidenhair Tree with Golden Fall Color)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring or fall in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun; Golden Girl is a female selection grown both as an ornamental for its reliable golden fall color and, once mature, for its edible ginkgo seeds (nuts).

directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun, watering regularly through establishment; mature ginkgo are exceptionally tough, tolerating heat, drought, pollution, and compacted urban soils. Golden Girl is a female cultivar selected for its exceptionally reliable, uniform golden-yellow fall color, a trait less consistent in many seed-grown female ginkgo trees. As a female clone it requires a nearby male pollinator, such as Autumn Gold, Princeton Sentry, or a wild male seedling, to produce fruit; once fertilized, the fleshy, apricot-colored seed coat that develops in autumn is notoriously foul-smelling and messy as it drops and decomposes, so site Golden Girl away from walkways, patios, and parking areas. Beneath that odorous flesh, however, each seed contains an edible kernel (ginkgo nut, or ginnan) that is a prized ingredient in Chinese, Japanese, and Korean cuisine, roasted or simmered in dishes like chawanmushi and used in soups and stir-fries; harvesters typically collect fallen seeds while wearing gloves, since the fleshy coating can cause skin irritation, and cure the cleaned seeds before cooking. Ginkgo is essentially free of serious pests and disease, and little pruning is needed beyond removing dead or crossing branches while young.
